analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by all law enforcement and ties federal police grants to anti-profiling policies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2004 with 16 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make racial profiling by federal, state, and local law enforcement a civil rights violation that individuals could sue over in court. Federal agencies would have to adopt written anti-profiling policies, collect data on stops and searches, and discipline officers who profile. State and local police departments would have to certify they have such policies and data collection in order to keep receiving major federal grant money, and the Justice Department would have to publish annual public reports on profiling nationwide.
analysis.who_benefits: Racial, ethnic, and religious minorities who are disproportionately stopped, searched, and questioned by police would gain a federal cause of action to sue for court orders stopping the practice. Communities broadly would gain access to public data on who is being stopped and searched, and honest officers would gain clear standards and complaint procedures.

how_it_helps.text: Makes racial profiling by any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agency illegal, and lets individuals injured by it sue in state or federal court for declaratory or injunctive relief [S2][S3].

Statistics showing a jurisdiction's stops and searches have a disparate impact on minorities count as prima facie evidence of a violation, and prevailing plaintiffs can recover attorney's fees [S2][S3].
Federal agencies must maintain anti-profiling policies, collect and report data on routine stops and searches, investigate complaints independently, and discipline agents who profile [S2][S3].

State, local, and tribal governments must certify they have such policies and data collection to keep receiving Byrne, COPS, and Local Law Enforcement Block Grant funds, with the Attorney General withholding grants for noncompliance [S2][S3].
Collected data must be available to the public, and the Justice Department must issue annual reports to Congress on profiling nationwide [S3].

The bill cites Department of Justice data showing searches of Black and Hispanic drivers produced contraband far less often than searches of white drivers, arguing profiling wastes police resources and undermines public trust in law enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies bear the costs of collecting and reporting stop data, building complaint and discipline systems, and potential grant withholding for noncompliance. Police departments and individual officers, their supervisors, and their governments would face new civil lawsuits and court-ordered reforms. Taxpayers fund the grant programs that would now carry these conditions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and governments facing suits

drawbacks.text: The bill lets statistics alone establish a prima facie violation and allows suits against individual officers and their supervisors, which law enforcement critics could argue would expose departments to frequent litigation based on demographics rather than proven intent [S3].

Collecting detailed data on every stop, search, and arrest, and acquiring cameras and record systems, imposes real administrative and technology costs, particularly on small departments, though the bill reserves grant funding for small and rural agencies [S3].

The definition covers reliance on race 'to any degree' and extends to immigration and customs enforcement, so agencies could argue it constrains lawful investigative tools they believe are necessary for border and national security work [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: minority drivers and pedestrians would stop being stopped and searched at rates unexplained by actual contraband findings, at the price of compliance costs for police departments and more civil litigation against them. The bill is designed to cushion those costs with federal grants for training, cameras, and data systems rather than only mandates. The main honest objection is procedural: disparate-impact statistics as prima facie evidence and supervisor liability make lawsuits easier, which could push departments toward defensive paperwork rather than better policing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Russell Feingold introduced the bill on February 26, 2004, with 13 original Senate cosponsors [S1][S3][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
Sixteen senators cosponsored it in total: 15 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and their governments, which kept their existing stop practices, faced no new data collection, complaint procedures, discipline requirements, or civil liability. Officers and agencies that engage in profiling are better off because no federal prohibition or enforcement mechanism took effect.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: One Senate Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican support

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a hearing, markup, or vote after its referral; the record shows no committee action for the remainder of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred, but support was nearly all Democratic: 15 of the 16 cosponsors were Democrats, one was a Republican, and the bill died without action in the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, local, and tribal police)
industries.note: The bill strips departments of discretion over profiling, requires stop data collection and public reporting, mandates complaint and discipline procedures, conditions federal grant money on compliance, and exposes departments, officers, and supervisors to civil suits. Their interest in avoiding oversight and liability runs against the public's interest in equal treatment by police.

Governments would face new civil liability and could lose Byrne, COPS, and block grant funds for noncompliance, but would also gain federal grants for training, cameras, and data systems. Their institutional interest in avoiding suits and conditions pulls against public accountability.

Best-practices grants could fund in-car video cameras, data collection systems, early-warning software, and training programs, creating demand for compliance technology. That interest runs alongside the public's interest in better-monitored policing.
